Colorful objects are put in the home of a male bower bird. Interesting animals live all through the world. Some of those animals look strange. Some of those animals have special skills. Come and see these wonders of nature.

An archerfish spits water. The water hits bugs. The bugs fall down into the water. The archerfish catches the bugs there. Then the archerfish eats them. The home of a trap-door spider is a tunnel. That tunnel is in the ground. A hidden door covers that home. The door is made from silk and dirt. Inside the tunnel, the spider stays hidden. Hunting is the reason it stays there.

Beavers chew through tree trunks. Dams are what they build. Trees are used in the dams. Mud is used in the dams. Stones are used in the dams. Chameleons change color. Hiding is one reason for a change. Showing how they feel is another reason.

A flying dragon has skin along its sides. That skin opens in the way wings do. The flying dragon jumps from tree to tree. A glide carries it between the trees. A leaf insect has body parts that match leaves. It matches the real leaves very well. Those real leaves are on trees.

A leaf is rolled by the female leaf-rolling weevil. She makes the leaf into a cone. The eggs she lays go into that cone. The leaf hides her eggs. The leaf protects her eggs. Prayer is the position of the front legs on a praying mantis. Five eyes are on a mantis. The eyes help the mantis hunt. Food is what the hunt is for.

Moles dig tunnels. Finding worms is why they dig. Eating the worms comes next. Tiny eyes are what a mole has. A mole is not blind. A side view shows the nest of a mole. The same view shows the tunnels. Small fish are what sea dragons are. The look of an ocean plant is theirs. Catching food is one use of the leafy parts. Hiding from enemies is the other use.

Many shapes show up in these animals. Many sizes show up in these animals. Each animal here is a wonder of nature. Dams are walls. Water cannot flow past a dam. A glide is a smooth move. A glide is a quiet move. A glide can go through air. A glide can go through water. Nature is the natural world. Animals are part of nature. Plants are part of nature. Land is part of nature. Silk is the name for threads. A spider makes silk. A caterpillar makes silk.

Come see some of the most amazing hotels. One stop is Skylodge Adventure Suites in Cuzco, Peru. One stop is the Hôtel de Glace in Quebec, Canada. One stop is Giraffe Manor in Nairobi, Kenya. One stop is the Treehotel in Harads, Sweden. One stop is the Sala Silvermine Hotel in Sala, Sweden. One stop is Jules' Undersea Lodge in Key Largo, Florida. One stop is the Tundra Lodge in Manitoba, Canada.

Cuzco, Peru, is the first stop, in the Sacred Valley. The hotel there is Skylodge Adventure Suites. Sleeping happens high up in the air. A view comes with the room. Canada is the next stop, at the Hôtel de Glace. Say the name like O-tel DEH GLAHS. Ice is what many hotel parts are made from. A warm fire can burn inside the ice hotel. Ice is used for the cups as well.

The bed for sleeping is made of ice. Spring makes the ice melt away. Each winter, workers put the hotel back up. Kenya is the next country after Canada. Forests around Giraffe Manor are home to giraffes. Breakfast may bring a visit from three giraffes. Every morning the giraffes visit the hotel. Eating is the reason they come.

A hungry giraffe may share the meal. Guests who stay can feed the giraffes. Sweden comes next on the tour. Many tree houses make up the Treehotel. One of them is called the Mirrorcube. Glass goes all the way around it. The glass helps it blend in with the woods. It sits up among the treetops.

A visitor climbs a ladder into the UFO tree house. A big bird nest is the shape of one tree house. The UFO house is shaped like a spaceship. It seems to come from outer space. The tour also stops at the Sala Silvermine Hotel in Sweden. Candles light the dark room under the ground. This room is the deepest hotel room in the world. The way down is long. Wear warm clothes. The mine is cold.

Florida holds the last stop, Jules' Undersea Lodge. Guests must swim down to reach the room. A window looks out into the water. Visitors can watch for fish through that window. A pizza can be ordered from the room. Someone from the hotel swims the pizza down. Sleeping there means fish are just outside.

Home is the place to go next. These hotels are more than places to sleep. Each one is incredible. Manitoba, Canada, is home to the Tundra Lodge. Big wheels make the lodge look like a train. Snow is the ground the lodge travels over. The ride takes visitors close to polar bears. Ice, trees, giraffes, a mine, and the sea were all part of the tour.

Spin a globe. Six continents are easy to find. The globe's lower edge is the place to look. Continent number seven is there. That continent is Antarctica. North America is number 1. South America is number 2. Europe is number 3. Africa is number 4. Asia is number 5. Australia is number 6. Antarctica is number 7. These seven lands are the continents. A globe helps you find each one.

An explorer’s ship got stuck in the ice in 1915. People now know much about this land. It is an amazing land. The South Pole lies in Antarctica. The tallest mountain there rises from the land. A piece of floating ice is as big as France. The South Atlantic Ocean meets this land. The South Pacific Ocean meets this land. The Indian Ocean meets this land. Antarctica is the coldest continent. It has the strongest winds. Less rain falls here than in other places. Less snow falls here than in other places.

Land and a floating ice piece meet. Water covers most of Earth. Almost all of that water is salt water. Most fresh water stays frozen inside Antarctica's ice. Even summer leaves the snow in place. More ice piles on as the years pass. Emperor penguins live in Antarctica. Freezing weather makes this place dangerous to live in. Summer does not clear the snow away. The ice grows thicker year by year. The cold stays over the land.

Grass grows in rocky places. Most plants live near the sea. Most animals live near the sea. Some of them live in the sea. Trees do not grow in Antarctica. Moss is one plant that does grow. A yawn opens the mouth of a seal on the ice. Penguins are among the larger animals here. Seals are among the larger animals here. The male emperor penguin's job is a large one. He cares for an egg for two months. He goes without food for the whole time. Then the mother comes back. She feeds the chick.

Study in Antarctica was opened up for scientists. A scientist studies a penguin chick. Antarctica is not under any one country's rule. Many countries stood behind one special agreement during 1961. The agreement does not allow wars there. Scientists stay indoors during blizzards. They can read while they wait. They can watch movies while they wait. Scientists are sent there by many countries. Some of those scientists work all year. Others work only in summer.

These scientists cut into the ice. They want to learn about the weather long ago. Antarctica draws scientists of many kinds. Some of them study animals. Some of them study ice. Some of them study other things. Most people visit during the summer months. Thousands of visitors come each year. Summer is the time for most trips. The cut ice can show old weather. Visitors arrive when the season is warmer.

Colorful clouds fill the sky. Antarctica is still mostly unknown to people. The cold makes a visit hard. The wind makes a visit hard. Rough seas make a visit hard. Still, people know this land should be protected. A continent is a main section of land on Earth. Dangerous means likely to cause harm. Frozen means turned into ice by cold. A globe shows the world as a round map. To protect means to keep something from harm. Scientists are people who work in science.

title: Brave Help on a Hard Day

pages.text: New York City faced an emergency on September 11, 2001. Planes hit two huge buildings called the Twin Towers. The buildings caught fire, and smoke drifted over the East River. People inside had to leave, and hurt people needed doctors. The fire left a mess that was not safe. Many brave heroes came to help. Volunteers fed those heroes during the day and during the night. Movie stars Susan Sarandon and Tim Robbins came to help. Many other people helped as well.

People walked out of a burning tower. Smoke filled the burning buildings. Using the elevators was not safe. An elevator carries people and things. It moves them from floor to floor. People hurried down the stairs. A man carried a woman who was hurt. Two men found a woman in a wheelchair. She was on floor 68. She needed their help. They carried her until she was safe. Many office workers helped someone else that day.

Not every hero was a person. Some of the heroes were dogs. About 400 dogs took part that day. Some dogs searched for hurt people. Some dogs searched for lost people. To rescue is to save someone from danger. Some dogs helped people feel better. Roselle was inside at the start of the fire. Her owner was Michael Hingson. He was a blind office worker. From floor 78 she led him outside. She brought him to a safe place. Michael Hingson hugged Roselle. Three dogs got medals. The medals were for facing danger that day. Roselle and Michael are shown at the far left.

Firefighters raced toward the burning buildings. They ran inside the towers. They put themselves in danger. They did it so they could save people. Other firefighters cleared the ground around the buildings. They moved people away from the danger. People were led away from one of the towers. Later the firefighters stood among the ruins. That spot is where the Twin Towers had stood.

Firefighters searched for people who needed rescue. They found people who were lost. They brought hurt people to doctors. One injured man got help from firefighters. A worker walked past the ruins of the towers. The burned buildings fell down. Broken walls sat in piles. Broken floors sat in piles. The piles lay all over the place. These ruins were not safe to be in.

Ironworkers came from many places. They came to help with the ruins. Ironworkers are builders. The towers had been built by some of these workers. Those were the towers that burned. They cut beams loose from the ruins. The beams belonged to the burned towers. They had to work carefully. Careful work was how they cleaned the ruins. Each day they faced danger. They worked until the mess was safe.

People offered thanks to the heroes of September 11. This emergency showed how brave people and dogs can be. They faced danger to keep others safe. Sometimes they felt afraid. Fear did not stop these heroes from helping others. People still offer thanks for that brave help.

The country of France lies in Europe. Spain is the country to the south. The United Kingdom is the country to the north. The English Channel lies between those lands. That channel belongs to the Atlantic Ocean. The Atlantic Ocean is also north of France. The Atlantic Ocean is west of France too. Other countries lie to the east. The map shows Belgium. The map shows Germany. The map shows Luxembourg. The map shows Paris. The map shows Dijon. The map shows Switzerland. The map shows Limoges. The map shows the Bay of Biscay. The map shows Italy. The map shows Bordeaux. The map shows Bayonne. The map shows Toulouse. The map shows Marseille. The map shows Monaco. The map shows the Gulf of Lion. The map shows Corsica. The map shows Asia. The map shows Africa. The map shows the Mediterranean Sea.

Paris has a famous tower called the Eiffel Tower. Say Eiffel like EYE-ful. Paris is the capital of France. The city is very famous. Each year, Paris gets millions of tourists. More than ten million people live in Paris. Many restaurants fill cities in France. People can eat outside at the restaurants. The population of France is more than sixty-six million. Most people live in cities. Most people work in cities. Some jobs help the tourists. Those tourists come to visit France.

Some farmers grow flowers. The flowers shown are sunflowers. The countryside is home to some people. They grow food on farms. Farmland covers more than half of France. Most people speak French. France has hills. France has forests. France has rivers. France has lakes. France has beaches. Low plains cover most of France. Hills are common there too. The map shows the Strait of Dover. The map shows the English Channel. The map shows the Seine River. The map shows Paris. The map shows the Brittany Peninsula. The map shows the Loire Valley. The map shows the Paris Basin. The map shows the Loire River. The map shows the Jura Mountains. The map shows the Bay of Biscay. The map shows Mont Blanc. The map shows the Massif Central. The map shows the French Alps. The map shows the Ligurian Sea. The map shows the Cote d'Azur. The map shows the Pyrenees Mountains. The map shows the Gulf of Lion. The map shows Corsica. The map shows the Mediterranean Sea.

No mountain in western Europe is taller than Mont Blanc. The French Alps are the home of Mont Blanc. Five mountain ranges are found in France. These ranges lie where France meets other countries. You find the highest mountains inside the Alps. Old stone castles stand across France. Long ago, this land was called Gaul. Time after time, other countries ruled Gaul. The Romans took Gaul first. Then the Franks took Gaul from the Romans. The name France comes from the Franks.

A painting shows Louis XIV. He was a powerful king of France. Say Louis like LEW-ee. Powerful kings ruled France for a long time. The people of France then fought one king. That fight was the French Revolution. The years were 1789 to 1799. Today the government is a democracy. On July 14, people watch fireworks in Paris. The fireworks are over the Seine River. Say Seine like SEN. July 14 marks the beginning of the revolution. People celebrate with fireworks. People celebrate with parades.

People in France enjoy many kinds of cheese. They eat crêpes. Crêpes are thin pancakes. Say crêpes like KRAYPS. A long, thin loaf of bread is called a baguette. Say baguette like ba-GET. People know France because of the food. A meal often has more than one part. A meal may include soup. A meal may include salad. A meal may include a main course. Fruit may be the dessert. Lavender is a type of flower. People grow lavender in parts of France. France is a beautiful country. It has a long history. The land has rolling hills. The land has forests. The land has mountains. People around the world know the food. Which part of France do you like the most?

The population is 66,259,012. The land covers 620,427 sq km. That is 239,548 square miles. The capital city is Paris. The primary language is French. The currency is the euro. Say euro like YUR-oh. A course is one part of a meal. A democracy is a government run by the people. Plains are large stretches of flat land. Plains usually have few trees. A range is a row of mountains. The mountains in a range are connected. A revolution removes a government by force. Another government takes its place. Enjoyment is one reason a tourist takes a trip. Tourists may also travel to learn.

Girls play soccer together in Arizona. This sport goes back a very long time. Soccer belongs with the oldest sports. Soccer belongs with the most popular sports too. People play the game all over the world. People in the United States call the sport soccer. Football is what most other places call it. The two names are for the same sport.

The top picture shows a match from 1905. Goalkeepers in caps guard the goal. The bottom picture shows a match from 1930. Goalkeepers guard the goal in that match too. Today's soccer rules were written in 1863. People called the game Association Football. British schoolboys made up a shorter name. They said assoccer. Say that name AY-sawk-ur. The name soon got shorter still. People said soccer. Some people call the field a pitch. A goal stands at each end of the field. Two teams play on the field. The ball is round. The field is large. Each team tries to send the ball into the other goal.

The goalie watches the ball. He guards his team's goal. Goalkeeper is another name for a goalie. Only a goalie may touch the ball with hands. Only a goalie may use arms on the ball. Other players use their chests. Other players use their feet. Other players use their heads. Other players use their legs. Kicking is how they move the ball on the field. A trap is a stop of the ball. A foot can make that stop. A knee can make that stop. A chest can make that stop. A player can head a ball that is up in the air.

A player dribbles in an Under 11 match. The match is in Cape Town. Cape Town is in South Africa. Dribbling is running with the ball. The player uses short, quick taps. Each tap kicks the ball to himself. The team with the ball is on offense. That team is trying to score. Defense tries to keep a score from happening. Defense also tries to take the ball away. Each team plays offense many times in a match. Each team plays defense many times too. Games like soccer are more than 2,000 years old. In those old games, feet sent a ball over a field. Ancient China loved these games. Ancient Greece loved them too. Ancient Rome loved them too.

The referee watches to see that rules are kept. A player may not push someone on the other team. A player may not hold someone on the other team. A player may not trip someone on the other team. Breaking a rule is a foul. The referee can call the foul. The other team may get a free kick. The other team may get a penalty kick. Most players need little special equipment. Cleats are one special item they use. Shin guards are the other special item. Cleats go on the feet. Players wear them to run on the grass. The cleats help them keep from slipping. Shin guards protect the legs.

A player stands at the side of the field. The player throws the ball in from there. The ball had gone out-of-bounds. The throw sends the ball back into play. Both hands begin behind the head. This kind of throw is special. Another player gets ready for a shot at the goal. Each goal gives the team one point. The winner is the team with more goals at the end. A tie means the teams finish with the same goals. After a tie, play may go on until someone scores. Teams may take penalty kicks instead. They take those kicks in turns. The kicks can pick the winner.

Players from the two teams shake hands after the match. Players get great exercise from this sport. Playing the game brings lots of fun. Players learn to work as a team. They learn to be good sports. Chasing the ball takes a very healthy player. More than 7 miles is often how far a professional runs in one game. Those 7 miles equal 11.2 km. Cleats are athletic shoes. Studs stick out of the bottoms. The studs help the wearer avoid a slip. A foul is an action against the rules. A player can get a penalty for that action. A goal is the place a ball must reach to score. In some games a puck must reach that place. A match is a game between teams. Dribbling moves the ball forward. The feet tap the ball over and over. The feet may also bounce the ball. A tie means the points end up the same.

title: A Happy Day for the Dead

pages.text: A boy in Lima, Peru, does a scissors dance. This dance is a tradition for Día de los Muertos. The name means Day of the Dead. People in many places celebrate this holiday. In Mexico, holidays like it go back thousands of years. People in the United States hold parades. They hold celebrations too. The usual days are around November 1 and November 2.

Día de los Muertos can look like Halloween. The two holidays are not the same. Halloween is often used to scare people. Joy is the heart of Día de los Muertos. People remember loved ones who have died. They celebrate those loved ones too. In Mexico, a family visits a loved one's grave. The family decorates the grave. Flowers are brought to a cemetery. Food is brought there too. Mexico is where Lidia Terán-Cooper grew up. Each year her family spent this day at the cemetery. They brought flowers. They brought a picnic.

The family told stories about people who had died. Bands played songs made for the day. In a cemetery in Mexico, a band plays. Lidia danced with the other children all day. The children played all day too. For Lidia, the day was always happy. The United States is Lidia's home now. Every year she and her family walk in a parade. The parade is in Tucson, Arizona. One puppet rises above the crowd. Many puppets fill that Tucson parade.

Lidia makes masks before the parade. Children paint the masks. Adults paint the masks too. People wear the painted masks in the parade. Dancers in San Antonio, Texas, wear painted skull masks. They show the masks in a Day of the Dead parade. In Tucson, Arizona, children wear many costumes. They walk in a parade made for children. Some places hold a parade only for children. The children decorate wings made of cardboard. They wear the wings. Paint goes on their faces. Costumes go on their bodies.

Other traditions also belong to this holiday. Altars get built inside some homes. Cloth covers the altars. Photos of the dead person are placed on the altar. A favorite item may be added. A piece of clothing may be added too. One altar in a home is set up for a loved one. Another altar is decorated with special bread. Other foods are on that altar too. Candles burn in a ring around the altars. They make the special bread. A favorite drink may be left there. Flowers decorate the altars. Skeleton toys decorate them too. Dolls decorate them as well.

Some people make skulls out of sugar. Colorful frosting covers the sugar skulls. Children love to eat these sweet skulls. A market in Mexico shows handmade sugar skulls. Art for the holiday often shows skeletons. Bright colors fill that art. Paintings of the holiday are made by some artists. The paintings show skeletons that dance. The skeletons play music too. The art honors friends who have died. It honors family members who have died too.

This holiday helps people feel better after a loved one dies. A parade can help them celebrate that person. Decorating an altar can help too. Life fills this holiday more than any other. Costumes fill the day. Masks fill the day too. Joy fills it. Memories fill it. Love fills it. Children perform at a festival in Los Angeles, California. An altar is a table or another raised surface. People may use it for a religious purpose. They may use it for a spiritual purpose. To celebrate is to do something special. That act honors an event. Dead people are buried in a cemetery. To decorate is to add color or an ornament. This makes a thing look nicer. To remember is to think of something again. It means you do not forget. Traditions are beliefs or customs. People pass traditions down.

title: A Look at the Grand Canyon

pages.text: Many people count the Grand Canyon as a wonder of nature. People around the world see it as a natural wonder. The canyon lies in the Arizona desert. A person in space can still see this very big canyon. Arizona is part of the United States. Phoenix is in Arizona. The North Rim runs along one side. The other side is the South Rim.

A canyon is a big valley with steep sides. A river usually makes a canyon. This park covers about 1,900 square miles of land. That is 4,921 square kilometers. Some spots drop more than one mile. That is 1.6 kilometers. A trip by river boat can take two weeks. The rocks in the walls are millions of years old. Theodore Roosevelt was a president of the United States. He was the first president to start work to keep this canyon safe. In 1919 the canyon became a park for the whole country. A park like that is a special place. The land there is kept safe. The animals there are kept safe too. Look up! Huge birds live here. People call them California condors. These birds almost died out. People caught the birds and kept them safe so they could have babies. Today more than five hundred of these birds live in the wild.

Time helped shape the Grand Canyon. Erosion helped shape it too. Erosion happens when small bits of ground wear off. The Colorado River flowed over this land for millions of years. The water wore the earth down. A deep canyon was left. Bottom rocks go back almost two billion years. The river still wears away soil. It still wears away rock. It still wears away other materials. Each day the canyon grows deeper. Bands of color stripe the canyon. Those bands are layers of sediment. The layers settled one on top of another. Settling went on for many years. Each layer tells how Earth has changed. The walls hold nearly forty layers of rock.

Native people still live in the Grand Canyon. The Havasupai are one group. The Navajo are one group. The Hualapai are one group. The Hopi are one group. The Zuni are one group. The Apache are one group. Life today is not the same as life for relatives long ago. Many stories have been passed to younger people. Traditions have been passed down too. People have lived in this place for at least twelve thousand years. Native groups have hunted here. They have built homes here. They have grown food here. Many tribes still live in this area. In the 1850s, settlers knew little about this place. In 1869 John Wesley Powell led a trip through the canyon. Local people taught him about the canyon's past. His group was the first to write that history down. Powell later led a second trip on the river. He also helped make maps of the area.

Making the canyon a national park pushed local tribes out. For many years the tribes had to stay away. Some Native people now help keep the canyon safe. They also help keep its history safe. Many favorite viewing spots sit on the South Rim. The South Rim draws large crowds. People can visit the South Rim on every day of the year. The North Rim is across the canyon. Most people must drive a long way to reach it. The North Rim stands much higher up. More snow falls on the North Rim. It is open only in the warmer months. Waterfalls pour in the low part of the canyon. Colorful pools sit down there too. Mules carry some visitors down into the canyon. Millions of people visit the park today. Some hikers spend many weeks exploring.

Raft trips on the Colorado River are a favorite. The river can be rough. The river can be fast. The river can be rocky. The trip is a grand adventure. About 277 miles of river twist through the canyon. That length is 446 kilometers. A tour guide can help visitors on the rafts. Rescuers help more than 250 people here each year. People who want a short hike can use easier rim trails. Many people love walks along the rim. They look out over miles of walls. Some walls are red. Some walls are yellow. Moving shadows cross the cliffs. A glass bridge called the Skywalk reaches over the canyon. The view from the bridge is amazing.

Big horn sheep live in the Grand Canyon. They are one of many animals kept safe here. This canyon is one of the great sights of nature. Its land will be kept safe for years to come. Its peoples will be kept safe. Its animals will be kept safe. Its history will be kept safe. A visit brings an adventure. A visit brings a view like no other. Winter makes the park a beautiful sight. Here are some words to know. Erosion means nature carrying rock or soil away. Water can do this. Wind can do this. Ice can do this. A national park is land the government keeps safe. It may be saved for history. It may be saved for wild land and wildlife. Native means belonging to a place by birth. Protected means kept safe from harm. Sediment means tiny bits of dirt and rock. Water, wind, or ice can move those bits. The bits later settle in a new place. Tribes are groups of people who share a way of life. They share land as well.
How fast can you run? How fast can you swim? Next to some animals, humans are slow. Which animals are the fastest?

A cheetah's body is built to go fast. The body is thin. A long tail helps it steer as it runs. The cheetah is the fastest runner. A car on a highway is a match for that speed. It can hold that speed for only a short time. It sprints in order to catch prey. Gazelles are a different animal. Wide open land is the usual home for gazelles. Open land makes them easy to spot. They can often outrun predators. Cheetahs eat gazelles. A gazelle is not quite as fast as a cheetah. A gazelle keeps a fast run going for longer.

Who is fastest on land? A human can run 20 mph. That is 32 kph. A gazelle can run 50 mph. That is 80 kph. A cheetah can run 70 mph. That is 112 kph. Australia is the home of this tiger beetle. It runs so fast that its eyes cannot do their job. Its brain cannot do its job either. It stays blind until it stops running. A big animal is often faster than a small one. Some small animals are fast for their size. The tiger beetle runs 170 body lengths in one second. A human who could do that could race a jet plane.

Sea turtles are fast in the water. They are strong swimmers too. Some of them travel thousands of miles during one year. A turtle is slow on land. Still, the fastest reptile in the world is a turtle. This turtle's swim is four times a person's swim. Sailfish and swordfish are hunters in the sea. Sailfish catch smaller fish. Then they eat those fish. Swordfish do the same. No animal in the sea is faster than the sailfish. In a race, it can beat most motorboats with ease. The swordfish is its cousin. The swordfish comes very close to that speed.

Who is speedy in the sea? A human swims at 5 mph. That is 8 kph. A turtle swims at 22 mph. That is 35 kph. A sailfish swims at 68 mph. That is 110 kph. Flight is a different kind of travel. Bats are the only mammals that can truly fly. Flight is the fastest kind of travel. Birds are among the fastest animals. Bats are among them too. Insects are among them too. Dragonflies are the fastest insects. They catch other insects that fly. Then they eat those insects. A dragonfly can fly backward. Its wings let it move sideways. Its wings let it hover in place.

Sharp eyesight helps a falcon hunt. No animal on Earth is faster than the peregrine falcon. A dive from above is how it hunts other birds. The wings pull in close while the dive lasts. Then it sails straight down. Who is fastest in the air? A dragonfly can go 60 mph. That is 96 kph. A Mexican free-tailed bat can go 60 mph. That is 96 kph. A peregrine falcon can go 242 mph. That is 389 kph.

An ostrich cannot fly because its body is too big. It can run 45 mph. That is 72 kph. No runner on two legs is faster than that. A cheetah's run can match the pace of a car. A motorboat loses to a sailfish in the water. An airplane's speed is a match for a falcon's dive. Animals can reach amazing speeds. Amazing means causing great wonder or surprise. Compared means looked at for sameness or difference. Prey is an animal that a predator hunts and eats. To sail is to move through the air in a smooth way. Speed tells how quickly something moves. It also tells how quickly something happens. To sprint is to go as fast as possible. A sprint is usually for a short distance.

Numbers are stuck to the backs of these racing snails. The numbers help people tell one snail from another. Some animals in the world move very slowly. The snail is one of the slowest. Even a fast snail is still pretty slow. In 1995, Archie the snail crawled 13 inches. That distance is 33 cm. The time for that crawl was two minutes and twenty seconds.

The Galapagos tortoise lives on the Galapagos Islands. South America is nearby. The Atlantic Ocean is nearby too. So is the Pacific Ocean. North America is on the same map. A walking person goes eighteen times faster than the Galapagos tortoise. The tortoise is not fast. It can live a long time. A tortoise life may last 150 years or even longer. The desert gila monster matches that tortoise in slowness. Gila is said HEE-luh. Its range includes the United States and Mexico. The map marks CA, NV, UT, AZ, and NM. The Pacific Ocean is on that map too. The gila monster tries to avoid humans. It tries to avoid other animals. If it is scared, it hisses loudly. Then it bites quickly.

Starfish are also called sea stars. Many kinds of sea stars fill oceans all over the world. Snails are not the only slow animals. A starfish seems not to move at all. At top speed, it only creeps. A move as long as a man's arm takes four minutes. The three-toed sloth lives in South America. The Atlantic Ocean and the Pacific Ocean are on its map. Most of the time, the sloth hangs in trees. It seldom moves. Its fur is often a home for little plants. A crawl as long as two cars takes about three minutes.

How long would each animal take to travel the length of one school bus? A snail would take 45 minutes. A gila monster would take 3 minutes and 15 seconds. A three-toed sloth would take 3 minutes and 15 seconds. A tortoise would take 3 minutes. A slow loris would take 25 seconds. A swallowtail butterfly would take 8 seconds. A woodcock would take 6 seconds. Seahorses live in shallow, warm ocean places. Those places have lots of plants. Four small fins sit on the bony little seahorse. It cannot swim fast. It cannot escape an enemy. So it hides. It wraps its tail around a branch. Then it looks like part of the plant.

The giant swallowtail is yellow and black. No butterfly in North America is larger than this one. Its range includes Canada, the United States, and Mexico. The Atlantic Ocean borders that range. The Pacific Ocean borders it too. Slow flaps come from the big wings of the large swallowtail. First it flaps. Next it glides. Then it flaps once more. It flaps about 300 times in one minute. It flies about twice as quickly as a six-year-old walks. The Greenland shark lives near Greenland. Its range includes North America and Europe. It lives in the Atlantic Ocean. This slow shark looks for sleeping seals. It also looks for dead whales to eat. People picture sharks as hunters that are fast. No fish in the ocean is slower than this shark. Very cold water is where this shark lives. It must use energy to stay warm.

The loris is careful. The loris is little. It has big eyes. At night it sneaks toward its food. It moves through tree branches very slowly. The slow move makes no sound. The slow loris lives in Asia. Its range includes the Philippines and Indonesia. The Indian Ocean is nearby. The Pacific Ocean is nearby too. This animal is endangered. Southeast Asia rainforests are where it lives. Sleep usually comes for it in the daytime. It hunts at night. Four types of manatees live in coastal waters. Those waters are around the world. All four types are endangered. Manatees are large. They are gentle. They are mammals of the ocean. They float along. Some people call them sea cows. They prefer not to rush. They munch on sea grass. In one hour of eating and floating, a manatee goes about three miles.

Some of these animals can go faster when they need to. Some move slowly only to save energy. Sometimes that energy is needed to heat the body. Sometimes their food gives them little energy. Slow animals do not win many races. They still have a way of life that works for them. Her baby is held by a three-toed sloth. She hangs from a branch as she holds it. Avoid means you stay away from a person or a thing. To creep is to move slowly. Creeping is often close to the ground. It can keep an animal from being noticed. Energy is the power to do work. It can make a change. It can move objects. A mammal is warm-blooded. A mammal has a backbone. They have hair or fur. They nurse their young. Their babies are born live. Seldom means not often. To sneak is to move so you are not noticed.
Some animals are the biggest of all. The height of a giraffe matches a two-story house. Two pickup trucks equal the weight of one elephant.

Some animals are the smallest of all. Water in one spoon weighs more than a bee hummingbird. The Chihuahua is one kind of little dog. The dog is small enough to fit in a pocket. Some animals are the loudest of all. A blue whale's cry is as loud as a rocket.

A big land turtle has a very long life. It can live for 150 years. One type of falcon dives at airplane speed. A mayfly has a very short life. It lives for only one day. An ostrich can match a horse in a run.
A kangaroo can keep its balance on its tail. All four feet can kick. Each zebra wears a different stripe pattern.
The eyes of a snake never close. A lizard can grow a new tail. The new tail grows if the old tail breaks off.

A butterfly tastes food with its feet. A penguin swims fast with its wings. A penguin cannot fly. A tiny hummingbird can fly backward. A cricket has ears on its knees. An ostrich eye is bigger than its brain. The picture shows the ostrich brain and the ostrich eye. These notes are fun facts about birds.

Sizes are not the same for every extreme animal. They come in many shapes. They almost call out for you to look. A house may be no taller than one of them. One may wear bright pink feathers. Some of them make a lot of noise. These wild animals stand out in the animal world. Which other extreme animals can you name?

Clouds gather above Lake Itasca. The lake is in Minnesota. Rain falls on the lake. The rain mixes into clear river water. The young river is small. Wading across is easy for a child here. This is how the mighty Mississippi River begins. Lake Itasca is only one name for the start. The Ojibwe people lived here first. They called the lake Omashkoozo-zaaga'igan. The map shows Canada. The map shows Wisconsin. The map shows Minneapolis. The map shows the United States. The map shows Iowa. The map shows Illinois. The map shows Mexico. The map shows the Upper Mississippi River. The map shows St. Louis. The map shows Missouri. The map shows Kentucky. The map shows the Lower Mississippi River. The map shows Tennessee. The map shows Arkansas. The map shows Memphis. The map shows the state of Mississippi. The map shows Louisiana. The map shows New Orleans. The map shows the Gulf of Mexico. The map shows the Mississippi River states.

The water travels for three months. The trip is 2,350 miles long. That length is 3,781 km. The water passes through ten U.S. states. At the end it reaches the Gulf of Mexico. A watershed is land that drains into a river. A watershed can drain into a lake. This watershed of the Mississippi River is huge. It is the fourth largest watershed in the world. Other rivers add their water to the Mississippi. The Missouri River is one of those rivers. The Missouri beats the Mississippi in length. A lock in Minnesota can raise a boat. The same lock can lower a boat. Then the boat can go around the dam. The boat keeps going along the Mississippi. At first the river passes dozens of locks. It also passes dozens of dams. Locks and dams raise the water near boats. They also lower that water. The change lets boats travel safely. They hold water back. Then boats do not hit the river bottom. The map shows the Ohio River.

In Iowa, a barge is filled with ground corn. A barge counts as a large kind of boat. The boat has a flat bottom. The boat carries goods. A barge can haul a big load. A semi truck hauls less. One barge equals 15 train cars. One barge also equals 58 trucks. Corn travels south by boat on this stretch. The boats carry soybeans south too. Shipping takes much of this food all around the world. The upper river is home to mammals of more than fifty kinds. Play is what river otters love in this spot. The number of fish kinds here is at least 260. One fish is the pallid sturgeon. Very few fish on Earth are older. Across 70 million years, it has stayed almost the same.

The Arch at St. Louis stands near the river. The Missouri meets the Mississippi 8 miles north of it. The 8 miles equal 13 km. The Missouri comes from the west. Its water is muddy. It mixes with the clear Mississippi. The Mississippi then turns brown. The Mississippi also grows wide. For the next 190 miles, wild animals are common. That part of the trip is 306 km. Nests of bald eagles sit in the tall trees. The eagles eat fish from the river.

The Ohio River joins the Mississippi. The Ohio comes from the east. The meeting place makes three state borders. Illinois is one of the states. Kentucky is one of the states. Missouri is one of the states. The river grows deep. The river grows even wider. In many places it is 1.5 miles across. That width is 2.4 km. The Mississippi is famous for floods. Damage from floods can be very great. Not every flood is bad. Floods leave rich soil on the banks. The soil helps farming. In 2012, a street in New Orleans was under water. A girl crosses that flooded street. A man helps her. She is the daughter of a neighbor.

More cities stand along this part of the river. New Orleans is in Louisiana. Boats here carry iron. Boats carry steel. Boats carry rubber. Boats carry wood. Cotton from the area rides on the boats. Other farm crops ride on the boats too. Some goods go north, back up the river. Some goods go farther south. A floating log holds a resting alligator. The log is in Louisiana. Several kinds of turtles live in this part. Alligators live here too. At times, people go swimming in this river. Martin Strel swam its full length. His swim was in the summer. The year was 2002. He comes from Slovenia. Long-distance swimming is what he does. Minnesota was his start. Louisiana was his finish. Sixty-eight days was the time it took.

A view from space shows the river. In the picture the river comes from the top left. It meets the Gulf of Mexico at the bottom left. The river's last stop is the Gulf of Mexico. Rain that fell at Lake Itasca left three months ago. That water has reached the sea. Someday some of the water may come back as rain. The rain may fall on Lake Itasca. The water may make the whole trip again. It may make the trip once more after that. A dam is a barrier. A dam stops water from flowing on. A flood is water over land that is usually dry. Too much rain can make a flood. A lock is a part of a river with gates. A lock can also be part of a canal. Water in the lock is raised. Water in the lock is lowered. Boats pass when the water changes. Mammals are warm-blooded. Mammals have backbones. Mammals have hair or fur. Mammal mothers nurse their young. Their babies are born live. This major river runs in the United States. The water path begins in Minnesota. The water path ends at the Gulf of Mexico. Shipped means goods were moved. A large boat is one way to ship goods.

Days grow shorter in this season. The air turns colder. Leaves fall away from the trees. Then the geese head south. The season now is fall. Winter will arrive before long. Snow will lie over the land. Ice will lie over the land.

The geese travel south in groups. Each group is a flock. A warmer place is where they are going. They rise up into the sky. They line up in the shape of the letter V. That line is a formation. This long trip is migration. A V formation helps them cover long distances. The shape lets them slip through the air more easily. They cut the air the way a knife does.

The goose at the front works hardest. The birds take turns in that front spot. A tired leader drops back. A goose from behind moves forward. This is how the flock shares the hard work. Sometimes one goose is injured. The injured goose has to stay where it is. Another goose stays there with it. The helper waits until the injured goose is well.

The injured goose grows strong again. Then it goes on with the migration. The goose that waited goes on too. A flock of geese is like a family. They look after one another. If one goose needs help, the others come. If one goose is in danger, the others are there.

The traveling geese reach a warmer place. They find lakes that are free of ice. They find rivers that are free of ice. They find ground that is free of snow. Plenty of food is there to eat. They stay until northern days grow long again. They stay until northern air grows warm again. They stay until northern trees grow fresh leaves. They stay until northern grass begins to grow.

The time to migrate comes again. On this trip the flocks turn toward the north. The new season is spring. Snow in the north has melted. Ice in the north has melted. Food in the north is plentiful. Spring has come to that land.

The geese choose mates. They build a nest together. The female lays the eggs. Baby geese will arrive soon. The babies hatch from the eggs. A baby goose is called a gosling. Parents care for the goslings. Parents teach the goslings how to fly. Before long, another migration will begin.

People live in a shared place called a community. People work there too. People play there too. A city is a large community. A town is a small community. A village is a small community too. People run the community with a government. The people in the government belong to the community.

Leading the community is the job of the mayor. A person who wants to be mayor runs in an election. A vote is how people make a choice. A mayor is picked when people vote. The election comes every two or four years. Each voter chooses the person who seems best for the job. The winner is the one who gets the most votes.

The Department of Public Works takes garbage away. It keeps the city clean. The mayor is in charge of many departments. The police department is one of them. The fire department is one of them. The mayor usually leads the council. The council decides how money is spent. It may build or fix roads, buildings, and parks. People share ideas at council meetings.

Keeping roads clear is work for the Transportation Department. Clear roads help drivers travel safely. The mayor and the council make laws together. Laws are important. Laws help keep people safe. Laws help keep the community clean. Car speed is limited by some laws. Other laws say not to throw trash on the ground.

Police officers watch to see that laws are followed. People who break a law may go to court. A judge may decide if someone broke the law. A jury may decide if someone broke the law. The top person at court is the judge. Community members can sit together as a jury. The jury listens to one side. The jury listens to the other side. Then the jury decides about the law. Sometimes there is no jury. Then the judge decides. If the person broke the law, there is a punishment. The judge decides the punishment.

Other government workers help the community too. Fires get put out by firefighters. Firefighters move people away to safety during a fire. Sick people get help from emergency workers. They help people who are hurt. A ride to a hospital may be part of that help. The community government is important. Every day, this work matters in people's lives. The government gives people a good place to live. The government gives people a safe place to live.

People can change their government by taking part. Entering an election is something they can do. A vote is one step they can take. Community meetings are a place where they can speak. They can offer to help in parks. They can offer to help in other places. What can you do to help your community? A community can be people in the same place. A community can share similar interests. A community can share similar qualities. A council is a group chosen to be in charge. Departments are separate parts of a big group. A department may be part of a government. A department may be part of a business. A department may be part of a university. An election picks a person for a government office. The pick is made by voting. A government can lead a city. A government can lead a state. A government can lead a country. A government can lead another area. Leaders in a government make decisions. They make sure laws are followed. A mayor leads the government of a city or a town.

title: A Maya City Called Chichén Itzá

pages.text: Stone animal heads are carved on many buildings in Chichen Itza. About three hundred buildings stand there. About fifty thousand people once lived in the area. Long ago, ancestors of the Maya people built a city in the jungle. The city is named Chichen Itza. Say chee-CHEN eet-SAH. The name means at the mouth of the well of Itza. This city is an important place in Maya history.

Chichen Itza is on the Yucatan Peninsula in Mexico. Say yoo-kah-TAHN. A few big cities share the peninsula. Most of the land around the old city is jungle, forest, and farms. The Maya people built this city many hundreds of years ago. They made stone buildings that still stand today. A tall stepped pyramid is the center building. The stepped pyramid rises ninety-eight feet.

A stone ring may have been the target in an old Maya ball game. The Great Ball Court is a wide field. A stone wall borders it. A rubber ball was the play piece. Elbows were allowed to move it. Hips were allowed. Knees were allowed. Hands were not allowed. Different Maya groups did the building. Hundreds of years went into the city. Low shape marks the older buildings. Flat shape marks them too. Bottoms often use plain stones. Tops often use fancy carved stones. The stepped pyramid does not match that older look. The Great Ball Court does not match it either. Tall columns carry carved animals. The older style shows in Casa de las Monjas. Nunnery is what that name means.

Newer style shows in the Temple of Warriors. Stone columns around it number about two hundred. A serious reason guided the Maya to this spot. Rivers are missing in this part of Mexico. Lakes are missing too. Underground wells called cenotes send fresh water up. Say say-NOH-tayz. Two cenotes belong to Chichén Itzá. Later, many people left the city. A few stayed. The close fresh water made the spot a fine home. Fresh water is one reason the cenotes matter. Religious use is the other reason.

Gold has been found by scientists in one cenote. Far travelers likely brought gifts. The rain god was the one honored. Drinking water came from one cenote. Gifts used the other cenote. Chac received those gifts. Chac is the rain god. Pleased by gifts, Chac would send rain, the Maya believed. Corn would grow because of rain. Other vegetables would grow too. Many important gods fill Maya culture. Temples make up many buildings here. Gifts for the gods can be given in a temple. The stepped pyramid carries a temple on top. A winged snake is the look of that god. Creation is the role of this Maya god. The Temple of Jaguars has a stone throne at the door. Jaguar shape is the throne shape. The jaguar matters greatly to the Maya people.

A market in Guatemala holds a walking Maya woman. Children walk with her. Old cities still have many Maya people living near them. Language count for the Maya is more than thirty. House words sound alike across Mayan languages. Sun words sound alike. Time words sound alike. Mother words sound alike. Corn words sound alike. Sky watching is still a Maya practice. Planting time for crops is clearer because of the sky. Yearly visitors to Chichén Itzá number more than one million. Climbing the stepped pyramid was once allowed for visitors who wished it. The steps wore down as time passed. Danger grew in those steps. Mexico wants the building kept safe. Mexico wants visitors kept safe. Climbing the steps is not allowed today. Ninety-one steps climb each side to the top.

Statues like this one number about twelve at Chichén Itzá. Stomach platters are part of them. Offerings for the gods can rest on the platters. A world honor list includes this city. Its name is New Seven Wonders of the World. Skill of the Maya shows in the amazing buildings. Ancestors are the relatives who came before you. Carved means cut in a careful way. Stone or metal can be shaped into a statue that way. Columns are support posts for a building. Central America and southern Mexico are home to the Maya people. Stone pyramids are among their buildings. Temples are places for prayer to a god. Wells are deep ground holes for water, gas, or oil.
Kiyana is going shopping. She shakes dimes and pennies out of her bank. José will help her count the money. He puts the coins in a row and counts. The row ends at thirty-five cents.

Kiyana organizes the coins by value, dimes first. She skip-counts by tens, then counts pennies by ones. She has thirty-five cents, then finds more pennies. They do not want to count every new penny alone. They put the pennies with the counted money and start again.
They put one dime or ten pennies in each group. Each group is worth ten cents. Kiyana counts by tens and has fifty cents. José finds nickels and dimes in his bank. Kiyana will help him count.

They count dimes first because dimes are greater in value. José counts one coin at a time up to fifty-five cents. He finds more nickels and counts all his money again. Two nickels equal one dime, so each group is ten cents. Why not make every group worth five cents?

José has eighty cents in all. Tony counts dimes, nickels, and pennies one by one up to sixty-two cents. Two nickels have the same value as one dime. José does not make each group worth five cents. You cannot break a dime in half.

Leara has saved quarters, dimes, nickels, and pennies. She wants to organize her coins by their value. How would she organize her coins? Quarters are greater than dimes, and dimes are greater than nickels. The order is quarters, dimes, nickels, then pennies.
Tony shows groups that are each worth twenty-five cents. Two dimes and one nickel equal one quarter. Five nickels also equal one quarter. How many pennies would make twenty-five cents?

Leara puts down three quarters and then a nickel. Three quarters make seventy-five cents, and the nickel makes eighty. Eighty cents is a round number, so counting on is easier. She skip-counts the dimes by tens from eighty cents. She reaches one dollar and ten cents.

Leara groups nickels in pairs worth ten cents each. She counts the last pennies and has one dollar and thirty-three cents. She and Tony picked two ways, but others might be faster. Kiyana buys her brother buttons for thirty-eight cents. She pays the exact amount with three dimes and eight pennies.

José has four dimes and eight nickels, which make eighty cents. His sister loves puppies, and the picture costs fifty-eight cents. He pays with eight nickels and two dimes. That is sixty cents, so his change is two pennies. The picture plus the change equals the sixty cents he pays.

Tony buys a little mouse for his cat Sparky. He pays with five dimes, which make fifty cents. The mouse costs forty-three cents, so his change is seven cents. The mouse plus seven pennies equals the fifty cents he paid. Seven pennies equal one nickel and two pennies.

A hat for Leara’s sister costs fifty-seven cents. She pays with three quarters, which make seventy-five cents. Two quarters make only fifty cents, less than the price. Her change is a dime, a nickel, and three pennies. The hat plus the change equals the three quarters she paid.

The day of the party arrives. Tony, Leara, Kiyana, and José give out the presents. Their guests are very happy. The kids are happy they could count coins to buy the presents. The gifts cost forty-three, fifty-eight, thirty-eight, and fifty-seven cents.
An alligator is ready to attack. A caiman is shown on this page too.
One animal shown here is an alligator. A second alligator is shown here too.

All crocodilians have short legs. All crocodilians have long bodies. All crocodilians have long tails. Crocodilians come in four kinds. The four kinds have different jaws. The four kinds have different teeth. Sharp teeth belong to all of them. Each kind can be met on its own. An alligator has a short snout. An alligator has a broad snout. A crocodile snout is narrower than an alligator snout. Two large teeth stick out on a crocodile. A drawing shows what an alligator looks like. A drawing shows what a crocodile looks like.

Caimans live in Central America. Caimans live in South America. A caiman head is shaped a lot like a crocodile head. Gharials eat fish. Gharials live in India. A gharial has a long snout. A gharial has a narrow snout. A drawing shows what a caiman looks like. A drawing shows what a gharial looks like. A crocodilian is hard to see in water. Only the top of the head shows. Only the top of the back shows. People often think they see a floating log. During a swim, the eyes stick up out of the water. The nostrils stick up out of the water. Seeing still works while most of the body is under water. Breathing still works while most of the body is under water.

A large tail helps a crocodilian move through water. The tail is powerful. Webbed feet help it move through water. Under water, the ears close. Under water, the nostrils close. The closing keeps water out. The windpipe can be shut off. The mouth can open after the windpipe is shut. Water is not taken in with a breath. Crocodilians are fierce hunters. Strong jaws capture their prey. Some animals they eat are as large as a deer. Some animals they eat are as large as cattle. Some animals they eat are as small as a fish. Some animals they eat are as small as a bird. They will attack people too. They cannot chew their food. They may swallow the food whole. They may tear the food apart. Sometimes they drag an animal under the water. They do this to drown the animal. A crocodilian has powerful jaws. A crocodilian is a good swimmer.
A crocodile eats a fish for lunch. Crocodilians lay their eggs on land.
This page shows crocodilian skin. Special care goes to a baby crocodilian.

When you were born, your body was shaped a lot like it is now. You were smaller then. You had a head, legs, arms, and a torso. When you grow up, that shape will stay about the same. Some baby animals look nothing like the adults they become. A flower beetle is one insect here. A ladybug is one insect here. A tropical ant is one insect here.

These animals have a different life cycle. A life cycle is the series of changes in an animal's life. Insect life cycles are fascinating. Some insects pass through four stages. The stages are egg, larva, pupa, and adult. Say larva as LAR-vuh. Say pupa as PYOO-puh. Other insects pass through three stages. Life starts as an egg. The insect hatches as a nymph. Say nymph as NIMF. Then it changes into an adult. A walking stick is one insect. There are more than 800,000 kinds of insects. Butterflies, beetles, fleas, and flies are some kinds. Insects come in almost every shape. Most insects share a few traits. A flea is shown here.

A blue wasp is shown here. A beetle is shown here. Every insect has six legs. The body has three parts. Most insects have wings and can fly. Most keep the skeleton outside the body as a hard shell. Moth eggs may sit on a leaf. You can find eggs in many places if you know where to look. Most insects lay eggs near food they like. Moths and butterflies lay eggs under leaves. Dung beetles lay eggs in balls of animal poop. Many flies lay eggs on meat. Some insects lay eggs on other animals.

Many insects make special cases to guard their eggs. One insect puts foam around its eggs. You may see that foam in tall grass. People call the foam cuckoo spit. Many insects lay eggs in pools, ponds, or streams. Others lay eggs underground. Rarely, a female keeps the eggs inside her body. The eggs hatch, and the young are born alive. A female fruit fly is shown laying eggs. Most eggs hatch into a worm-like larva. Caterpillars, grubs, and maggots are larvae. Say larvae as LAR-vee. A larva has a long body and many legs. A larva can eat more than its own weight in one day. Newly hatched larvae may rest on a leaf.

Here is the larva of a black swallowtail butterfly. Many larvae can destroy crops. Some suck sap from crop roots. Others eat leaves, fruits, or vegetables. Beetle larvae can weaken and kill trees. Some moth larvae eat wool clothing. A silkworm is a moth larva. It makes silk thread. A grown larva must change its shape. It must protect itself while it changes. Many larvae spin silk cocoons or grow hard shells. The pupa does not eat and does not move much. Inside, the insect is busy changing shape. This change is called metamorphosis. Say it as MET-ah-MORF-oh-sis. Here is the pupa of a black swallowtail butterfly.

When metamorphosis is done, the pupa hatches as an adult. Many larvae that lived in water become adults that live on land. Larvae that lived underground come out above the soil. A comet moth is one adult. Adults find mates, and females lay eggs. For some insects, that is all the adults do. A mayfly adult lives for only one day. Most other insects live longer as adults. They eat, fly, hunt, and work. A stink bug nymph is shown here. Eggs in the three-stage cycle hatch as nymphs, not larvae. A nymph looks like a small adult. Some nymphs do not have full wings. A dragonfly nymph may live underwater.

Nymphs do not turn into pupae. They shed their skin as they grow. Each time they shed, they look more like an adult. Slowly, the nymph becomes an adult. An adult dragonfly is shown here. This is skin that a dragonfly nymph has shed.

The timber wolf is a second name for the gray wolf. Gray wolves belong to the mammal group. A thick coat of fur covers them. Each tail is long. Each tail is bushy. They grow larger than any other wolf. Hunting other animals makes them predators. Many kinds of places can support them. Some live on mountains. Some live in forests. Some live in deserts.

Shoulder height for an adult is usually just under a meter. About 3 feet is that same height. From nose to tail, length is almost 2 meters. More than 6 feet is that same length. A male often weighs around 45 kilograms. About 100 pounds matches that weight. A male may reach 65 kilograms. That top weight is 143 pounds. Females do not grow as large. Fierce hunting is part of gray wolf life. They can run at high speed. Their jaws are very powerful. Their teeth are sharp. The largest sharp teeth bite the animal being hunted. Other teeth crush bones. Other teeth cut meat. A coat may be all white. A coat may be all black. People still use the name gray wolf. The fur is not limited to gray. Colors in the fur run from white to black. One paw can match the size of a grown person's hand.

A female leader stands among the other members of her pack. A wolf is a social animal. Wolves live together in a group. That group is known as a pack. A usual pack holds six to ten wolves. Some packs on the move have reached thirty wolves. One leader in the pack is male. One leader in the pack is female. The offspring of those leaders live there too. The two leaders are known as alphas. Each wolf has a rank in the pack. The alpha male holds the highest rank. An alpha may bare its teeth at other wolves. Those wolves move away in fear. The male alpha and the female alpha sit together. Gray wolf alphas usually stay mates for life.

A gray wolf pack may surround an elk. The wolves prepare to attack. Large paws help wolves travel on snow. The paws let them move quickly. The paws let them move with ease. Hunting in a pack helps them take large animals. Deer are one large animal they hunt. Elk are another large animal they hunt. Moose are another large animal they hunt. Smaller animals are hunted as well. Rabbits are one smaller animal they hunt. Days can pass while a pack follows large animal groups. The wolves look for a weak animal. The wolves look for a hurt animal. Then the wolves hide. They surround one target. The leader gives a signal. The wolves attack after that signal. A lick can show respect to an alpha. Pack members communicate with all five senses. Ear position can send one message. Tail position can send a different message. They bark to share a message. They cry to share a message. They howl to share a message. They use smell with one another. They use licking with one another. No gray wolf howl sounds the same as another.

Her pups get a lick from the alpha female. She does this at the den entrance. A wolf den is usually a hole. Wolves dig that hole in the ground. A small cave can be a den too. Alphas mate from January through April. The female starts digging about sixty days after that. She digs a long tunnel. A den sits at the end of the tunnel. Four to six pups are born inside that den. New pups cannot see. New pups cannot hear. A soup can is about the weight of one newborn pup. The pups chase each other. The pups wrestle each other. This play is practice for learning to hunt. Nursing lasts about two months for the pups. After that, they eat warm meals of meat. Parents regurgitate that meat for them. Offspring stay with the pack for at least two years. Then they leave. Finding mates is why they go.

Long ago, a gray wolf howl often broke the quiet night. Free travel once took gray wolves all around the world. Over the past hundred years, much territory was lost. By 1926, people had killed off the gray wolves of Yellowstone National Park. That park is in the United States. A program started in 1995. Wolves returned to the park because of that program. Scientists wanted the wolves to hold elk numbers down. The goal was control of elk in the park. The park held about one hundred wolves during 2016. Those numbers continue to grow. Packs in the park have different names. One of them is the Gibbon pack. People built new towns. People built new cities. That building changed the land. People drove the wolves away. People also hunted wolves. They wanted to stop wolves from killing cattle. They wanted to stop wolves from killing sheep. Gray wolf numbers dropped in Europe. Gray wolf numbers dropped in the United States. In some places, the numbers are rising again. A world map can show gray wolf lands long ago. A world map can show gray wolf lands today. The 2010 source was the International Union for Conservation of Nature.

A gray wolf smells much better than a human. The wolf sense of smell is about one hundred times stronger. A large share of gray wolf territory is gone. They are getting some territory back now. Gray wolves live as social animals. A pack lives together. A pack hunts together. Gray wolves are top predators. They help keep the natural world in balance. Communicate means letting a thought or an idea be known. Words are one way to do this. Pictures are another way. Other means can be used too. A mammal is warm-blooded. A mammal has a backbone. A mammal has hair or fur. A mammal nurses its young. A mammal baby is born live. Offspring are the young of an animal. Offspring can be the young of a plant. Predators hunt other animals. Predators eat the animals they hunt. To regurgitate is to bring food back up. The food was in the stomach. The food returns to the mouth. A territory is an area that animals defend. The area can be land. The area can be water. Animals live in that area.

People in every land celebrate holidays. Traditions fill those holidays. A tradition is a special way people do a thing. People prepare food. People eat the food. People play games. People sing songs. People tell stories. Ornaments hang on a Christmas tree. Gift envelopes are for Chinese New Year. Bright colors are painted on the ground at Holi.

Late January or early February brings Chinese New Year. Many people celebrate it. They celebrate the arrival of spring. They wish for good luck. Good luck sayings go in the home. They watch a colorful Lion Dance. Loud noises chase bad luck away. People give gifts. It began in China. A lucky cloth lion dances in the street. One Christmas date is December 25. Another Christmas date is January 6. A family stays together on that day. It began in Europe. Some people pick a different day. Many people use December 25. The holiday is usually one day. The party may last longer. A tree is put in the home. Colorful lights cover the tree. People sing songs. Family gets gifts. Friends get gifts. People in need receive toys. They receive clothes. They receive food.

Middle December can start Hanukkah. Late December can start it too. Other people celebrate it. Eight nights is the length. One candle is lit each night. Each candle sits in a holder. That holder is a menorah. It began in the Middle East. Family hears the songs. Friends hear the songs. Family shares the food. Friends share the food. People receive small gifts. People receive money. The gifts get shared with others. The money gets shared with others. People play a game with a dreidel. A dreidel is a top. Holi comes during March. Some people celebrate it. Winter comes to an end. Spring starts at that time. Songs are sung. People dance. They decorate using lots of colors. Their clothes are colorful. Colorful powders land on family. Colorful powders land on friends. Water is sprayed as well. Joy is part of Holi. Fun is part of Holi. It began in India. Family members decorate one another.

Kwanzaa starts on December 26. Kwanzaa ends on January 1. Kwanzaa began in North America. Other people celebrate Kwanzaa. This time is important to friends. This time is important to family. Seven days is the length. People light candles each night. A kinara holds the candles. Seven candles stand in the kinara. One candle belongs to each night. People eat a meal together. People give gifts. An mkeka is set in the home. The mkeka is a mat. Vegetables are set on that mat. Special items are set on that mat. Traditional stories get told. Family hears the stories. Friends hear the stories.

January 1 is a New Year date. The start of spring is another date. Many celebrations use fireworks. It began in the Middle East. Every land marks the New Year. Calendars do not all agree. A calendar marks a year's start. Traditions for this day are many. Many people sing songs. People may toss colorful paper in the air. People wish others good luck. The wish is for the new year. The Western calendar changes the Ramadan date each year. A family eats together once Ramadan ends. Ramadan began in the Middle East. Other people celebrate it. It lasts one month. Many people eat before the sun comes up. Many people eat after the sun goes down. They do not eat between those times. People show thanks for things they have. People think about other people. People do nice things for them.

A holiday often feels special. People in many lands celebrate holidays. Some customs are not the same. Some customs are the same. Holidays come all year long. Chinese New Year lasts for 15 days. Christmas can fall on December 25. Christmas can fall on January 6. People mark that holiday every year. Christmas lasts one day. People often celebrate on extra days. Many people follow the Gregorian calendar. It is also called the Western calendar. Each year has about 365 days.

Holi covers 15 days. People celebrate it in March. A full moon falls on the day before Holi. People welcome the new year on the night before New Year's Day. The Muslim calendar guides Ramadan. That calendar has 354 days. Ramadan can last about 29 days. It can last 30 days. How many days is the Muslim calendar shorter than the Western calendar? How many days do Chinese New Year and Kwanzaa last altogether? A dreidel is a top for a Hanukkah game. A kinara is the candleholder for Kwanzaa. A menorah is the candleholder for Hanukkah. An mkeka is a mat for Kwanzaa vegetables.

Touching a stinging nettle makes a glove a necessity. Sharp claws belong to this Sumatran tiger. Sharp teeth belong to it too. Those parts help the tiger defend itself. Animals keep safe in many ways. Sharp claws are one way. Teeth are one way. Horns are one way. A color change is one way. Hiding in a shell is one way. Running from danger is one way. Biting is not possible for a plant. Fighting is not possible for it. Running away is not possible for it. Other protections still belong to plants. The book then tells how plants stay safe.

Needle-like thorns grow long on hawthorn branches. A thorn is a small branch from inside a woody stem. It may also grow from inside a woody branch. Branch thorns appear on some plants. An animal that tries to eat one may get cut. A scratch is possible too. Long thorns on some trees hold animals off. Sharp prickles grow on a rose. They form on the stem outside, in the way skin forms a layer. Stem prickles belong to roses and to some other plants. Prickles and thorns are not the same. A prickle comes out of a soft stem. Small shrubs are the usual prickle plants. Flowering plants are usual too. Trees or large shrubs are the usual thorn plants.

Many spines cover every barrel cactus. A fishhook curve tips some of those spines. Defense is the reason some plants grow spines. Being eaten is less likely under a spine coat. A spine can look like a thorn. A spine can feel like a thorn. The two are still different. Another name for the hairy cactus is the old man cactus. White strands like hair cover it. Sunlight is blocked by the strands. Sharp spines stay partly hidden because of the strands. A cactus spine is a leaf of a special kind. Hot deserts are the usual cactus home. A normal leaf may dry in that hot sun. Spines make sunlight bounce away. Spines make heat bounce away.

A stinging nettle drawing marks a breakage point. It marks stinging fluid. It marks the leaf surface. It marks the solid base of a hair. Another name for stinging nettles is common nettles. People have used them to treat muscle pain. Hundreds of years are behind that use. Hairs on stinging plants can poke an animal that wants to eat them. A small tube sits inside each hair. Stinging fluid sits in the tube. The tube tip breaks with ease. A painful rash can follow the fine hairs. A bump knocks the tip off. Fluid then shoots into the animal. Hundreds of stinging hairs cover each nettle leaf.

Berries on deadly nightshade may seem fit to eat. Strong poison is what they hold. Poison is a protection some plants make. Sickness can follow a bite of the plant. Death can follow too. Powerful poison comes from deadly nightshade. Every plant part holds that poison. Only one leaf is enough. A large animal can die from that leaf. People like the smell of peppermint. People like the taste too. Insects are harmed by it. Poison in a plant does not reach every animal. Rocks can hide a living stone plant by matching it. The middle plant in a photo does this blend. Some plants hide by matching the ground they grow in. Dry rocky ground, with pebbles and stones, is the living stone home. It seems to be only one more small stone. Animals do not treat it as food.

The name touch-me-not fits the plant. Contact makes the leaves shut. A before view shows open leaves. An after view shows the change. A bump from an animal makes the leaves fold. Folded thin leaves look less tasty than full ones. Motion in a plant may scare an insect. Another hungry animal may be scared too. The tobacco hornworm is hunted by the big-eyed bug. A chewed tobacco leaf sends a smell that draws the bug. Pests that eat the tobacco plant meet a trick. A bite on a leaf releases a special smell. Enemies are invited by that smell. The big-eyed bug is such an enemy. The bug eats the insect that invaded the leaf.

The closing picture shows a prickly pear cactus. It shows a New Mexico thistle. It shows an agave. A first look may suggest a plant cannot defend itself. Powerful defenses are still there. Survival is what those defenses support. Claws are absent. Horns like animal horns are absent. Protection is still possible. Defend means to resist an attack. A fluid is a liquid. Water is one fluid. Poison is a toxic substance. Harm or death can follow if it enters the body. Swallowing is a special risk. A prickle is a sharp point on a soft stem. Small shrubs grow prickles. Plants that make flowers grow them too. A spine is shaped like a needle. A spine is really a leaf. A cactus is one example. A thorn is short and sharp. It grows out of a woody branch. Large shrubs grow thorns. Trees grow thorns.

title: I Am the Planet You Live On

pages.text: I will introduce myself. My name is Planet Earth. No planet in our solar system is luckier than I am. I can support life. Take a look at Mercury. Mercury sits very close to the Sun. It is hot there. That heat is too much for even a single desert rat of mine. Pluto is a dwarf planet. Pluto is cold. Pluto sits very far from the Sun. Would you want to be a planet frozen solid? I would not want that.

I hold everything life needs. Land is one thing I have. Water is one thing I have. Air is one thing I have. Energy from the Sun is one thing I have. I have five oceans. I have seven huge pieces of land. People call those pieces continents. Lakes on my land hold fresh water. Rivers on my land hold fresh water. Plants need that fresh water. Animals need that fresh water. My spin is like the spin of a top. The spin gives every living thing a day. The spin gives every living thing a night. People call this spin rotating.

You can test what makes day and night. Get a flashlight. Ask a friend to play the part of the Sun. You play the part of Earth. Turn around slowly. Daytime is on the side of you that faces the Sun. The side that faces away from the Sun has nighttime. A ball and I share a round shape. Sunlight does not hit my round body evenly. That uneven light makes some parts hot. That uneven light makes some parts cold. Direct sunlight falls most strongly on my belly. The hottest band follows my belt. People call that band the equator.

My North Pole gets the least direct sunlight. My South Pole gets the least direct sunlight. Rays from the Sun are weaker there than at my equator. Those pole areas are my coldest places. Creatures live on my hot parts. Creatures live on my cold parts. Creatures live on the parts in between. People live on every one of my continents. The area around my South Pole has a few people. Antarctica is the land around that pole. Most people live where I am milder. Homes can be built in those milder parts. Crops can be grown in those milder parts.

People travel all over me. Long ago, people got lost while sailing my oceans. They needed a way to identify locations. So they invented a global grid. Lines cross to form points anywhere on me. The lines that run north and south are longitude lines. The lines that run east and west are latitude lines. This grid tells people where they are. I am tilted too. As I travel around the Sun on my yearlong trip, I stay in my tilt. Sometimes I tilt toward the Sun, and sometimes away from it. My tilt creates seasons. In January, my top half, the northern half, is tilted away from the Sun. That is winter, when children there go sledding. At the same time, the southern half points toward the Sun. It is summer there.

Halfway around the Sun, the month is July. I am still tilted then. This time my northern half tilts toward the Sun. Summer is the season in the northern half. My southern half points away from the Sun. Winter is the season in the southern half. I am a fair planet. I give seasons to each half. I give each half an equal share of sunlight. The two halves get that light in different parts of the year. I make a promise to all life on me. A full turn of mine takes 24 hours. Daytime will come from that turn. Nighttime will come from that turn. I will keep my tilt. Seasons will keep coming from that tilt. Each year I travel once around the Sun. Billions of years will not stop me from doing these things.

I am a planet you can trust. Antarctica is an ice-covered continent around the South Pole. Continents are the great divisions of land on me. They are Africa, South America, Asia, Europe, North America, Australia, and Antarctica. The equator is an imaginary line that circles me halfway between the North Pole and the South Pole. Latitude is distance in degrees north or south of the equator. Longitude is distance in degrees east or west of an imaginary line running north and south through Greenwich, England.
